summary: A change raises an allowance in the legacy baseline (`nitpicker.legacy.json`).
why: The baseline records old problems so that they can shrink; raising it would hide new ones.
allowed: Fix the new sites instead of baselining them.

exception.note: It has no exception: fix the sites instead of raising the allowance of the legacy inventory.

summary: A callback breaks its protocol: `source-loader-does-not-merge-published-state`, `publication-owner-does-not-commit-external-state` or `correlated-callback-declares-correlation-input`.
why: Callbacks that belong together keep one owner for the state they publish and declare the input that correlates them. No contract is declared by default, so the rules report only where a callback contract is configured.
allowed: Commit published state in its owner, read only bounded metadata or independent upstream snapshots in a loader, and declare the correlation input in the options.

summary: A doc comment that only restates its declaration name, or whose description is longer than the limit.
why: A comment that repeats the name adds noise; a long one belongs in names and types.
allowed: Delete the comment, or say what the name cannot: a unit, a limit, an edge case or why. TypeScript and JavaScript report this as `nitpicker/no-comments`.
limit: a doc comment that only restates its declaration name, or a description longer than 5 lines, code examples not counted (TypeScript and JavaScript report it as `nitpicker/no-comments`)

summary: A method of an exported interface that a production class implements, which no production code outside the implementations uses.
why: A contract method that production code never calls is dead surface that every implementation has to carry.
allowed: Remove the method from the interface, or call it from production code.

summary: A module breaks the runtime boundary of its role: `forbidden-runtime-dependency`, `forbidden-runtime-call` or `unresolved-runtime-dependency`.
why: Module roles keep the runtime dependencies and side effects of each layer in one direction. No role is declared by default, so the rules report only where a role is configured.
allowed: Depend on the allowed module, move the call to a module whose role may make it, and write the specifier of a dynamic import as a string literal.

summary: A module under a shared root that exactly one feature reaches and nothing else uses.
why: `shared` is for code several features use; code with one user belongs with it.
allowed: Move the module into the feature that uses it.

summary: A package that depends on a less stable package.
why: Stable code that depends on volatile code breaks whenever the volatile code changes (the Stable Dependencies Principle).
allowed: Depend on an abstraction in a more stable package, or move the dependency inward. An import that exists only for the type checker is never the reported dependency.

summary: A branch the change added or touched with coverage below the minimum.
why: Only changed code is held to coverage, so a change cannot add code that no test exercises.
allowed: Cover the branch with a test. When a branch cannot be reached from a test, accept it with an exception that names its function; it applies to that function only.
limit: a changed branch with coverage below 95%

summary: A function with unknown coverage and so no CRAP score, because no test runs it.
why: A function no test runs cannot be scored, and is the riskiest kind.
allowed: Add a test that calls it; for inline composition-root wiring, move it into a named function and test that.

summary: A function whose CRAP score (its complexity combined with how little of it the tests cover) is at or above the limit.
why: Complex code that tests do not cover is the code most likely to break unnoticed.
allowed: Test the uncovered branches, or split a branchy part into its own function.
limit: CRAP score at or above 9; override with `QUALITY_CRAP_SCORE_LIMIT` (positive number) or `thresholds.crapLimit`

summary: Unused export.
why: An export that nothing imports is dead surface; every reader has to understand it.
allowed: Remove `export`, or the declaration if nothing uses it.

summary: Unused file.
why: Nothing imports the file, and no entry point, test or configuration reaches it.
allowed: Delete the file, or import it where it is needed.

summary: An export, module or main class that only tests use (a re-export is not an import).
why: Code that only tests call is not part of the product, and its tests prove nothing about it.
allowed: Remove `export` or make the declaration private, move a test-only module to a test-support folder, or use it from production code.

summary: Unused exported type.
why: An exported type that nothing imports is dead surface; every reader has to understand it.
allowed: Remove `export`, or the type if nothing uses it.

summary: An import of a package that `package.json` does not list.
why: An unlisted package works only by accident of what else is installed.
allowed: Add the package to the right dependencies of `package.json`.

summary: An import that resolves to no file and no package.
why: It fails when the code runs.
allowed: Fix the path, or install the package and list it in `package.json`.

summary: A dependency in `package.json` that nothing imports or runs.
why: Unused dependencies add install time and attack surface.
allowed: Remove it from `package.json`.

summary: A new block of code that repeats another block, also when only the names and literals differ.
why: Copies drift apart and each fix has to be made twice.
allowed: Extract the shared code into one function or module and call it from both places. When the copies are meant to be copies, the message names the files to add to `exclude`.
limit: jscpd in `mild` mode, also over sources with names and literals normalized (at least 100 tokens, except code that only repeats one or two statements); any new clone fails

summary: An import that goes around the public entry point of a package.
why: Importing internals defeats the entry point that keeps a package replaceable.
allowed: Import from the public entry point.

summary: A mutant in code that no test runs.
why: Code no test reaches is not protected against change.
allowed: Add a test that runs the code and asserts its result.

summary: A mutant (a small deliberate change to production code) that every test survived.
why: A mutant that survives shows a test that runs the code without checking what it does.
allowed: Strengthen the test so that it fails for the mutant: assert the exact value instead of only running the code. An equivalent mutant is accepted with an exception after review.

summary: A change to `nitpicker.config.json` or to a tool config that makes the gate check less than the base did.
why: A change that loosens the policy it is judged by would pass itself, so a person has to accept it.
allowed: Keep the base's policy and change the code until it passes: keep new code under the source roots, where the gate checks it, and fix findings instead of excluding, excepting or reclassifying the code.

exception.note: It has no `exceptions` entry. Only a person reviewing the change accepts exactly these loosenings, with `--accept-policy-change=<digest>` at an interactive terminal or `NITPICKER_ACCEPT_POLICY_CHANGE=<digest>` in CI.

summary: A committed archive or compiled binary (`gradle-wrapper.jar` is allowed).
why: Binaries bloat the history, cannot be reviewed and go stale.
allowed: Remove the file; fetch or build it in the build instead.

summary: A committed build output folder (`dist`, `build`, `out`, `coverage` or `target` next to a project manifest; `.next`, `.nuxt`, `storybook-static`, `.turbo` or `.parcel-cache` anywhere).
why: Build output is generated, so committing it creates noise and merge conflicts.
allowed: Remove the folder from version control and add it to `.gitignore`.

summary: A committed `.env` file (templates such as `.env.example` are fine).
why: An env file holds real secrets and values that differ per machine.
allowed: Remove the file from version control, ignore it, and commit a `.env.example` template.

summary: A committed private key: a key file, or any text file holding a private-key block.
why: A key in git is a leaked key.
allowed: Remove the key from the repository, rotate it, and load it from a secret store or the environment.

summary: A committed file larger than the limit (lockfiles are exempt).
why: Large files bloat every clone for ever.
allowed: Keep large data outside the repository (artifact storage, Git LFS).
limit: a file larger than 1 MB (lockfiles are exempt)

summary: A class with more instance fields than the limit.
why: Many fields mean a class holds state that belongs in separate types.
allowed: Group related fields into a record or a class of their own.
limit: more than 10 instance fields in a class of the main Java sources or the Python source roots; override with `thresholds.classFields`

summary: A class with more methods than the limit.
why: A class with many methods usually has more than one responsibility.
allowed: Split it into classes by responsibility.
limit: more than 20 methods in a class of the main Java sources or the Python source roots; override with `thresholds.classMethods`

summary: A component file without a story, in a package that has Storybook.
why: When most components have a story, a component without one is an oversight.
allowed: Add a story for the component. The rule is enforced only when more than half of the component files have one.
scope: The JavaScript preset enforces this check only in part.

summary: A used literal constant, function or type with the same name and text in two modules of a package.
why: Two copies of one definition drift apart.
allowed: Define it once in one module and import it where it is used.
scope: The JavaScript preset enforces this check only in part.

summary: Two different exports with one name, imported by the same module, which keeps the name for one of them.
why: Two things with one name make an import ambiguous to read.
allowed: Rename one of the exports.
scope: The JavaScript preset enforces this check only in part.

summary: A file longer than the limit (source and test files have separate limits).
why: Long files collect unrelated responsibilities and are slow to review.
allowed: Split the file by responsibility and put new code in a new file.
limit: more than 300 lines in a source file or 500 in a test file; override with `thresholds.fileLines` and `thresholds.testFileLines`

summary: Code nested deeper below its feature folder or root package than the limit.
why: Deep trees hide where code belongs and make imports long.
allowed: Flatten the tree: move the code up to the feature or package that owns it.
limit: code more than 1 folder below `features/<feature>/<layer>/` (TypeScript), more than 4 packages below the root package (Java, Kotlin) or more than 4 packages below the root package (Python); override with `thresholds.folderDepth`

summary: A folder with more source files, or more test files, directly in it than the limit.
why: A flat folder of many files has no structure for a reader to follow.
allowed: Group related files into subfolders (packages in Java and Kotlin).
limit: more than 6 source files, or test files, directly in one folder; override with `thresholds.folderFiles`

summary: A function that nests control flow deeper than the limit.
why: Deep nesting makes the paths through a function hard to follow and to test.
allowed: Return early instead of nesting, or move the nested part into its own function.

summary: A function longer than the limit.
why: Long functions hide several jobs in one place; agents grow them instead of splitting them.
allowed: Split it into functions named for what each part does and put new code in a new function. A function, file or class already over its limit may be edited as long as the change does not make it worse.

summary: A function with more parameters than the limit.
why: Long parameter lists are easy to call in the wrong order and tend to grow.
allowed: Group related parameters into one object (an options object, a record or a data class) instead of adding another.

summary: A function with more statements than the limit.
why: Many statements usually mean several responsibilities in one function.
allowed: Split it by responsibility and name each part for what it checks or does. A function, file or class already over its limit may be edited as long as the change does not make it worse.

summary: A class that extends more superclasses than the limit.
why: Deep inheritance spreads behaviour over many classes and couples them.
allowed: Hold the shared part as a field and delegate to it instead of extending.
limit: a class more than 3 superclasses deep in the main Java sources or the Python source roots; override with `thresholds.inheritanceDepth`

summary: A `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs` or `.jsx` file in a project that has a `tsconfig.json`.
why: JavaScript in a TypeScript project has no type checking.
allowed: Write the file as `.ts` or `.tsx`.

summary: A line longer than the limit, except imports, URLs and the text of string literals.
why: Long lines are hard to review in a diff and hide complexity.
allowed: Break the line up or extract a named value; a formatter wraps what it can.
limit: a line longer than 120 characters, except imports, URLs and string literal text; override with `thresholds.lineLength` (Java files: the width of the formatter, 100 for google-java-format and 120 for palantir-java-format, or the `java.lineLength` convention (a Checkstyle `LineLength` max, a pin, or measured when no formatter runs); Kotlin files: detekt's)

summary: A new icon-sized `.svg` file while an icon package is a dependency.
why: Icons from one package look consistent; one-off files pile up.
allowed: Use an icon from the icon package instead of adding a file.

summary: A component named like one the project already renders from a dependency.
why: A second copy of a library component diverges from the real one.
allowed: Use the library's component.
scope: The JavaScript preset enforces this check only in part.

summary: A function or class edited so that it drifts from its same-named copy in another module while that copy is left unedited.
why: Editing one of two near-identical copies leaves the other with the old bug.
allowed: Edit the copy as well, or merge the copies into one.
limit: a function or class edited so that it drifts from its same-named copy in another module of the package, at least 80% the same tokens before and after, while that copy is left unedited

summary: A property of the options parameter of an exported function that no call sets; in Kotlin, a defaulted parameter of a private or internal function that no call names or fills.
why: An option nobody sets is dead surface that every reader has to understand.
allowed: Remove the option, or set it from a real call.

summary: A prop the project declares that no caller passes (a spread of a non-literal passes all).
why: An option or prop nobody sets is dead surface that every reader has to understand.
allowed: Remove the prop, or pass it from a real caller.

summary: A test file that prints console error or warn output the base run did not print.
why: Console noise hides real warnings and usually points at a leaked timer or an unhandled error.
allowed: Fix the cause of the output, or allow a third-party message in `testConsole.allow` of nitpicker.config.json.

summary: A test that runs no production runtime code.
why: A test that never runs the code it is named for cannot fail when that code breaks.
allowed: Import and run the production code the test is about.

summary: A test the change adds or edits that takes longer than the limit for its kind (unit or integration).
why: Slow tests slow every run and are the first to be skipped; most tests should be fast unit tests.
allowed: Make the test fast: inject a clock or a fake instead of waiting, or move it to the integration tests, which have a higher limit.
limit: a test the change adds or edits taking more than 5 s (unit) or 30 s (integration); override with `thresholds.unitTestSeconds` and `thresholds.integrationTestSeconds`

summary: A test whose only link to production code is a type-only import.
why: A type import proves nothing at runtime, so the test cannot fail when the code breaks.
allowed: Import and run the production code the test is about.
